turns.text: Good morning, Doctor. I'm Mateo Aguilar-Recinos. My family doctor sent me here. I've had these light-brown birthmarks since I was a kid, and over the past ten years I've gotten more and more soft lumps on my skin. Lately one bigger lump deep in my left thigh has been aching and seems bigger. My mother had similar spots and bumps before she passed. I just figured it was a skin thing, not something serious.

Thank you for coming in, Mr. Aguilar-Recinos. What you are describing is not simply a skin condition. The combination of childhood pigmented patches, multiple soft nodules appearing in adolescence and adulthood, and an affected first-degree relative raises strong concern for **Neurofibromatosis type 1**, historically called von Recklinghausen disease. It is a systemic genetic disorder, not a localized rash, and it is exactly the deep, growing, painful lesion you mention that I most want to characterize today. Let me start by clarifying the timeline. When did the pigmented patches first appear, and when did the soft nodules begin? And the deep left thigh mass, how long has it been growing and is the pain constant or triggered by movement?

The brown patches were there in infancy, my mother said some were present at birth. The little freckly spots in my armpits and groin showed up around age six or seven. The soft rubbery bumps on my trunk and arms started around fifteen and there are dozens now. The deep thigh mass I noticed maybe three years ago, but in the last four or five months it has grown noticeably and now there's a constant deep ache, sometimes a tingling shooting down my leg, even at rest and at night.

That history is important, and the recent change in the deep lesion is the part I take most seriously. Let me record your vitals and examine you systematically. Today: **BP 134/82 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, RR 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 C, height 174 cm, weight 78 kg, BMI 25.8**. On skin examination I count **more than 30 café-au-lait macules**, the largest measuring **22 mm**, well above the 15 mm threshold for adults. There is dense **freckling in both axillae and the inguinal folds (Crowe sign)**. I count numerous discrete **cutaneous and subcutaneous neurofibromas** over the trunk and arms, easily more than two dozen. Along the left posterior thigh I palpate a firm, deep, partly fixed mass approximately **8 by 6 cm** with a positive Tinel sign radiating down the leg. I would like ophthalmology to examine your irises with a slit lamp today. Have you had any vision changes, and do you know if a brain or eye scan was ever done?

No vision changes that I notice. I had headaches as a teenager but they checked out fine. No scans that I remember. Honestly the eye thing surprises me. What does my eye have to do with the bumps on my skin?

It is a fair question. NF1 affects multiple organ systems because the underlying gene is active throughout the body. The **NF1 gene** on chromosome 17q11.2 encodes **neurofibromin**, a protein that switches off the RAS signaling pathway. When one copy is lost, RAS/MAPK signaling runs unchecked, which drives tumor growth in nerves, pigment changes in skin, and benign growths in the iris. Those iris growths are **Lisch nodules**, melanocytic hamartomas visible only by slit-lamp. They cause no vision problems but are a diagnostic marker present in most adults with NF1. The slit-lamp exam today confirmed **bilateral Lisch nodules**. So far you meet the diagnostic criteria several times over: six or more café-au-lait macules, axillary and inguinal freckling, multiple neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, and a first-degree relative likely affected. That is a clinical diagnosis of NF1 without needing genetic testing to confirm it, although genetic testing has other uses we will discuss.
So I definitely have it. What about the big thigh lump, why does that one worry you more than all the little bumps?

Because the deep lesion behaves differently from your superficial nodules. Your small skin neurofibromas are benign and essentially never become cancerous. The deep thigh mass is more consistent with a **plexiform neurofibroma**, a tumor that grows along an entire nerve and its branches, often described as a bag of worms on palpation. Plexiform neurofibromas are present in roughly 30 to 50 percent of NF1 patients and carry a lifetime risk of transformation into a **malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST)** on the order of **8 to 13 percent**. The warning signs of transformation are precisely what you reported: **rapid growth, new or worsening persistent pain especially at night, new neurological deficit, and a previously soft lesion becoming hard or fixed**. Your four-to-five-month growth with constant nocturnal pain and radiating numbness is a red-flag presentation. This needs urgent imaging, not watchful waiting.
That is frightening. What imaging, and what happens if it is turning into cancer?

We move stepwise. First, a **whole-body or dedicated MRI with and without contrast** of the left thigh and pelvis to map the plexiform neurofibroma and look for features that suggest transformation: large size, irregular margins, central necrosis, and heterogeneous enhancement. The most useful functional test is an **18F-FDG PET-CT**; an SUVmax above approximately **3.5** raises suspicion for MPNST and helps target the most metabolically active region for biopsy. If imaging is worrying, we obtain an **image-guided core biopsy** of the hottest area rather than the whole tumor. If MPNST is confirmed, the cornerstone of treatment is **wide surgical resection with negative margins**, which offers the best chance of cure, often combined with **radiotherapy**, and **chemotherapy** for high-grade or metastatic disease. The regimens used in that setting include agents such as **ifosfamide with doxorubicin**, and for some nerve-sheath protocols agents like **carboplatin and vincristine**. If it remains a benign but symptomatic, inoperable plexiform neurofibroma, there is now a targeted medical option I will describe.
Tell me about the targeted option. I'd rather take a pill than have surgery if I can avoid it.

The targeted agent is **selumetinib (Koselugo)**, an oral **MEK inhibitor** that blocks the downstream MAPK pathway driven by neurofibromin loss. In the **SPRINT phase 2 trial**, selumetinib produced durable partial responses in about **66 to 70 percent** of patients with symptomatic inoperable plexiform neurofibromas, with meaningful reductions in pain and improvement in function. I must be precise about its current label, however. **Selumetinib is FDA-approved specifically for children aged 2 years and older with symptomatic, inoperable plexiform neurofibromas.** In an adult like you, it would be used **off-label**, and only if your tumor is confirmed benign, symptomatic, and not surgically resectable. The pediatric dose is **25 mg/m2 by mouth every 12 hours**, and adult off-label dosing is individualized in a specialist center. It is not a substitute for surgery when MPNST is suspected. So our sequence is: characterize the lesion first, exclude malignancy, and then decide between resection and a MEK inhibitor.
If I did end up on selumetinib, what should I watch for? And does it interact with anything? I want to be careful.

Selumetinib has class-specific toxicities you would need monitored. The most important are **cardiac**: it can lower the heart's ejection fraction, so we obtain a baseline **echocardiogram** and repeat it periodically. It causes **ocular** effects, including retinal pigment epithelial detachment and rarely retinal vein occlusion, so ophthalmologic monitoring continues. **Dermatologic** rash is very common, along with elevated **creatine kinase**, diarrhea, nausea, and elevated liver enzymes. On interactions, the critical one: **strong CYP3A4 inhibitors such as itraconazole increase selumetinib exposure up to 2.4-fold**, which amplifies cardiac and skin toxicity, so azole antifungals like itraconazole and ketoconazole, and grapefruit, must be avoided. If you ever received **vincristine** as part of nerve-sheath chemotherapy, the same azole antifungals would also be dangerous there, because they inhibit its metabolism and markedly **increase vincristine neurotoxicity**. And if **carboplatin** were ever used, we would avoid concurrent **aminoglycoside antibiotics** because the combination is additively toxic to the kidneys and hearing. These are the specific combinations I flag for every NF1 patient on these agents.
Understood, no azole antifungals. For the nerve pain shooting down my leg right now, is there anything safe I can take? Over-the-counter stuff barely touches it.

The shooting, tingling, radiating quality tells me this is **neuropathic pain** from nerve involvement, which responds poorly to ordinary analgesics, exactly as you found. A reasonable agent is **pregabalin (Lyrica)**, starting at **75 mg by mouth twice daily**, titrated over one to two weeks to **150 mg twice daily** based on response and tolerance, with a usual ceiling of **300 mg twice daily**. Expect possible dizziness, drowsiness, peripheral edema, and some weight gain; dosing is reduced if kidney function is impaired. Importantly, pregabalin treats the symptom; it does not shrink the tumor or substitute for the imaging workup. Now, I need to ask directly about a few things that affect both your nerve pain and your overall risk. Do you smoke, drink alcohol, and are you taking any supplements, vitamins, or herbal products at all? Please be exact, because it genuinely changes my recommendations.
I don't smoke at all, never have. Maybe a beer on weekends. And no, I don't take any supplements or vitamins, nothing like that.

I appreciate that. I want to gently revisit one point, because the details matter for safety. When my nurse took your medication reconciliation in the waiting area, you mentioned a daily herbal capsule a relative brings you from Guatemala for energy and circulation. On the intake form it is listed as a St. John's wort preparation. I am not raising this to criticize you, many patients do not think of herbal products as medicines. But it is clinically important: **St. John's wort is a potent CYP3A4 inducer**, and any future MEK inhibitor or nerve-sheath chemotherapy would be metabolized faster and rendered less effective. So I do need an accurate list. Are you taking that herbal capsule?

...You're right. I'm sorry. I do take it, every morning. I didn't think of it as a real medicine, and honestly I worried you'd tell me to stop something that helps me feel better. It's the one from my aunt.

Thank you for telling me, and there is no need to apologize. Most people do not consider herbal products as drugs, so this is a very common omission, not a failing on your part. Here is why it matters concretely: **St. John's wort induces CYP3A4 and would lower blood levels of selumetinib or vincristine**, potentially making a future treatment fail while you believe you are protected. For now, I would ask you to stop the herbal capsule and we will address energy and mood directly if needed. Please keep me informed of anything your family brings you, even teas, because the metabolism of these drugs is the difference between a treatment that works and one that quietly does not. Now let me outline the full plan and the genetic and family implications, which are a major part of managing NF1 as a systemic condition.
Yes, please. And I have a question about my kids, I have a four-year-old daughter and a baby son.

That is one of the most important parts of this visit. NF1 is **autosomal dominant** with **complete penetrance but highly variable expressivity**, meaning each of your children has a **50 percent chance of inheriting the NF1 gene variant**, but the severity cannot be predicted even within the same family. Roughly half of cases are inherited and half arise from new (de novo) mutations. I recommend formal **genetic counseling** and **NF1 gene sequencing with deletion/duplication analysis**, which confirms your specific variant and, in a small subset such as large whole-gene microdeletions, predicts a more severe course with higher tumor burden. Once your variant is known, your children can be evaluated. Practically, your daughter and son should be examined by a pediatrician familiar with NF1: serial skin exams for café-au-lait macules, and annual ophthalmologic screening through childhood to detect **optic pathway gliomas**, which occur in about 15 percent of children with NF1 and are most relevant before age six. Your baseline lab panel today was unremarkable: **CBC normal, hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL (ref 13.5 to 17.5), platelets 245 x10^9/L (ref 150 to 400), creatinine 0.9 mg/dL (ref 0.7 to 1.3), ALT 24 U/L (ref 7 to 56), CK 110 U/L (ref 30 to 200)**, which gives us reassuring baselines before any MEK inhibitor.
So what exactly happens next for me, step by step? I want to be clear before I leave.

Here is the plan in order. **One:** urgent MRI of the left thigh and pelvis with contrast, plus whole-body MRI to map internal plexiform neurofibromas, scheduled this week. **Two:** FDG PET-CT to assess metabolic activity of the thigh mass; an SUVmax above about 3.5 prompts **image-guided core biopsy** of the most active region. **Three:** start **pregabalin 75 mg twice daily** now for neuropathic pain, titrating up as tolerated, and **stop the St. John's wort capsule today**. **Four:** baseline **echocardiogram** and a repeat dedicated ophthalmology exam, both to establish baselines should we proceed to a MEK inhibitor. **Five:** referral to **genetic counseling** with NF1 sequencing for you, and pediatric NF1 evaluation for both children including annual eye screening. **Six:** review at our multidisciplinary NF tumor board. If the mass is a benign symptomatic inoperable plexiform neurofibroma, we discuss off-label **selumetinib**; if imaging or biopsy indicates **MPNST**, we move directly to surgical resection with oncology. **Seven:** lifelong NF1 surveillance, including annual clinical exam and blood pressure checks, since NF1 also predisposes to hypertension from renal artery stenosis and pheochromocytoma. Do you have questions before we book the MRI?

One more worry. My job involves climbing, ladders, crawl spaces, working with my hands all day. If this is a nerve tumor in my leg, am I going to lose strength or feeling? Should I be doing anything differently at work right now?

A practical and important question. Right now your strength exam is intact: I documented **5/5 power in hip flexion, knee extension, ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion bilaterally**, with only mild reduced light-touch sensation over the lateral left calf along the lesion's nerve territory. That is reassuring, but a plexiform neurofibroma involving a major nerve can progress, and an MPNST can cause sudden motor loss. Until we have the MRI, I would not have you stop working, but I want you to be alert for specific warning signs: **new foot drop, a tripping or slapping gait, sudden weakness lifting your foot, numbness that spreads, or pain that escalates sharply**. Given your work at heights, even a transient leg weakness is a fall risk, so please avoid solo ladder and roof work until we image you, and report any new deficit the same day. We will fast-track the scan precisely so you are not left guessing.
That makes sense, I'll keep a coworker with me on the ladders. How often will I need to come back, and who all will be on my care team?

NF1 care is lifelong and team-based, which is why we run a multidisciplinary clinic. Your core team will include me as **neurogenetics**, a **genetic counselor**, **ophthalmology**, **surgical or orthopedic oncology** for the thigh lesion, **medical oncology** if systemic therapy is needed, and **neurology or pain management** for the neuropathic symptoms. Once the current lesion is characterized and stable, the baseline cadence is an **annual comprehensive NF1 visit**: full skin and neurological exam, **blood pressure check** at every visit given the pheochromocytoma and renal artery stenosis risk, and a directed history for new or changing masses. We do not perform whole-body MRI on a fixed routine in asymptomatic adults; instead, imaging is driven by symptoms or by a known plexiform neurofibroma that needs monitoring. Any new persistent pain, rapid growth, or neurological change triggers an interval scan rather than waiting for the annual visit.
Last thing. If selumetinib ends up being the plan, how long would I take it, and would the tumor come back if I stop?

Realistic expectations matter here. Selumetinib is generally a **continuous, long-term therapy** rather than a fixed course. In the SPRINT data, responses were durable while patients remained on treatment, with median time to response of several months and benefit maintained over years of continued dosing. It typically **shrinks and stabilizes** a plexiform neurofibroma and reduces pain, but it is **not curative**, and tumors can **regrow or symptoms recur after discontinuation**. So if we go that route, we would plan for ongoing therapy with the **echocardiographic, ophthalmologic, liver enzyme, and creatine kinase monitoring** I described, weighing benefit against toxicity over time. That is also why surgical resection is preferred when a lesion is operable, and why we must first exclude malignant transformation, because for MPNST the answer is surgery, not a MEK inhibitor. We will make that decision together once the imaging and, if needed, biopsy results are back.

turns.text: Hi doctor, I'm Mariana. I keep getting these terrible spinning spells. The whole room whirls and I have to lie down or I'll fall. It comes out of nowhere, lasts maybe half an hour to a couple of hours, and lately my right ear feels plugged up with this low roaring sound. I'm honestly scared something is seriously wrong with my brain.

Thank you for describing that so clearly, Mariana, and I understand how frightening unprovoked vertigo can be. The pattern you describe is very characteristic of an inner-ear process rather than a brain catastrophe, but I want to be thorough. Let me ask focused questions. When the room spins, is it a true rotational sensation, as if you or the room are turning, rather than lightheadedness or faintness? And during these spells, do you notice nausea, vomiting, or that your right ear becomes more muffled or full at the same time?

Yes, it is definitely spinning, like I am on a carousel. I get very nauseous and I have thrown up a few times. And you are right, my right ear gets worse, more muffled and full, right before or during the spell. Afterward I feel wiped out and unsteady for the rest of the day.

That clustering is important. Episodic spontaneous vertigo lasting **20 minutes to 12 hours**, with simultaneous fluctuating hearing changes, tinnitus, and aural fullness in one ear, forms the classic symptom complex of **Meniere's disease**. The underlying problem is thought to be **endolymphatic hydrops** — an abnormal accumulation of endolymph in the membranous labyrinth of the inner ear. Before I commit to that, how many discrete attacks have you had, over what time span, and roughly how long does each one last from start to finish?

Over the last four months I have had maybe seven or eight real attacks. Most last around 45 minutes to two hours. Between them I feel mostly normal, but my hearing in the right ear seems to come and go, and the roaring tinnitus never fully leaves now.

That history of at least two spontaneous episodes of vertigo each lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours, with documented low-frequency hearing changes and persistent aural symptoms, maps directly onto the **Barany Society / AAO-HNS 2015 diagnostic criteria** for definite Meniere's disease. To meet the definite threshold, I need to audiometrically document a **low-to-mid frequency sensorineural hearing loss** in the affected ear on at least one occasion. Let me first take your vital signs and do a focused neurotologic exam, then we will get formal hearing testing. Any history of migraine, head trauma, ear surgery, or autoimmune disease?

No ear surgery and no head injury. I do get headaches sometimes but not with visual auras or anything dramatic. My mother had bad arthritis but I don't think any autoimmune diagnosis. No other major medical problems that I know of.

Good. Your vital signs today are **BP 132/84 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 C**, and a fingerstick glucose of **96 mg/dL** (normal fasting 70-99 mg/dL). On exam, otoscopy shows normal, intact, mobile tympanic membranes bilaterally with no effusion or vesicles. Tuning fork testing with a 512 Hz fork: the **Weber lateralizes to the LEFT (better) ear**, and **Rinne is positive bilaterally (air conduction greater than bone conduction)** — that combination is consistent with a sensorineural loss on the right, not a conductive one. Let me continue with balance and eye-movement testing.
Okay. What are you looking for with the balance tests? Right now I am not in an attack, so I feel relatively steady sitting here.

Between attacks the exam is often near-normal, which is itself reassuring and typical. I am checking for signs that would point elsewhere. Your **Romberg is negative** with eyes closed, and tandem gait is intact. The **head impulse test (HIT)** shows a subtle corrective saccade on rightward thrusts, suggesting mild right vestibular hypofunction. I see no spontaneous nystagmus in primary gaze and **no direction-changing or vertical nystagmus** — vertical or purely torsional fixed nystagmus would raise concern for a central cause. **Dix-Hallpike maneuver is negative bilaterally**, which argues against benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. Cranial nerves, including facial sensation and strength, are intact, and there is no limb dysmetria. This is a peripheral, not central, picture.
That is a relief to hear it looks peripheral. So what tests come next to be sure?

Three things. First, **pure-tone audiometry** today to document and quantify the hearing loss. Second, an **MRI of the internal auditory canals and brain with gadolinium contrast** to exclude a vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma), other retrocochlear pathology, and demyelinating disease such as multiple sclerosis — this is essential because a one-sided sensorineural loss with tinnitus must never be assumed to be Meniere's without imaging. Third, vestibular function testing: **videonystagmography (VNG) with caloric irrigation**, and likely **VEMP** and **video head impulse testing (vHIT)**. Electrocochleography, which can show an elevated summating-potential to action-potential (SP/AP) ratio, is sometimes added as a supportive test.
I just finished the hearing test in the booth. The audiologist did not explain the numbers. What do they actually show?

Let me walk you through the audiogram. Normal hearing thresholds are **0-25 dB HL**. Your LEFT ear is essentially normal: **10 dB HL at 250 Hz, 10 at 500 Hz, 15 at 1000 Hz, 15 at 2000 Hz, 20 at 4000 Hz**, with **speech discrimination 100%**. Your RIGHT ear shows a classic **up-sloping low-frequency sensorineural loss**: **45 dB HL at 250 Hz, 40 at 500 Hz, 35 at 1000 Hz**, improving to **25 dB HL at 2000 Hz and 20 at 4000 Hz**, with **speech discrimination 84%**. Tympanometry is **Type A bilaterally**, confirming normal middle-ear pressure and no effusion. That documented low-frequency right-sided sensorineural loss is exactly what the diagnostic criteria require.
So it really is Meniere's. Is my hearing going to keep getting worse? And what can we do to stop these attacks? They are wrecking my job and I am terrified of having one while driving.

Pending the MRI to exclude other causes, your presentation meets criteria for **definite Meniere's disease** of the right ear. Honest prognosis: the hearing typically fluctuates early and may gradually become more permanent over years, and there is a **30-50% chance of the other ear becoming involved over a decade** — so we monitor both. The good news is that vertigo is controllable in the large majority of patients with a stepwise plan. Your driving fear is valid and clinically important: I will counsel you specifically on **fall and driving safety**, and warn you about rare sudden drop attacks — **Tumarkin otolithic crises** — where people fall without warning. If those occur, you must not drive until we have control. Let me start with how we abort an acute attack.
Yes please. When I am mid-spin and vomiting, what do I take?

For an acute attack we use vestibular suppressants and antiemetics for short-term relief only. I will prescribe **meclizine 25 mg by mouth every 6 to 8 hours as needed** during attacks (Antivert). For severe spells with intractable vomiting, **promethazine 25 mg orally or rectally every 6 hours** or **ondansetron 4 mg** helps the nausea, and a short course of **diazepam 2-5 mg** can calm an acute crisis. The important caveat: these are rescue agents only. Used chronically they cause sedation and actually impair the brain's vestibular compensation, so we do not use them daily. Lie down in a safe place, fix your gaze on a stationary point, and stay hydrated. The real work is in preventing attacks.
What does prevention look like? I want to get my life back.

The foundation is lifestyle, and the single most powerful lever is **dietary sodium restriction to under 1500-2000 mg per day**. Sodium drives fluid balance in the inner ear, and lowering it reduces endolymphatic pressure and attack frequency. We also reduce **caffeine, alcohol, and nicotine**, all of which can provoke attacks, and we work on stress and sleep, since both are common triggers. On the medication side, the mainstay prophylaxis is a **diuretic — hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg, often combined with triamterene 37.5 mg, once daily** to maintain a lower-fluid state; **acetazolamide 250 mg daily** is an alternative. Many clinicians also use **betahistine** — typically **16 mg three times daily or 24 mg twice daily** — which improves inner-ear microcirculation and is widely used outside the US. Now, to set realistic targets, walk me through what you typically eat and drink in a day.
Honestly I eat pretty healthy. Lots of rice and beans, some chicken, vegetables. I don't think salt is really my problem. Maybe one coffee in the morning.

I appreciate that, and rice and beans and chicken can absolutely be part of a healthy pattern. But the inner ear responds to the total sodium load, not the overall impression of healthy eating, so let me do a careful step-by-step recall rather than a general question — this is routine, not a test you can fail. Yesterday, specifically: what brand or form were the beans, did you add salt, sazon, adobo, or bouillon while cooking, were there any canned soups, deli meats, cheese, olives, or crackers, and how many cups of coffee, soda, or alcohol across the whole day, including the cafe con leche many people have in the afternoon?

Well... now that you ask it that way. The beans are canned, and yes I cook with adobo and a sofrito base, plus a chicken bouillon cube. There is usually ham or salami in the rice. I add extra salt at the table because my husband likes it. And okay, it is more like three cafe con leches a day, plus a soda, and a couple of beers on the weekend. I just didn't think it counted.

Thank you for being candid — that detail completely changes the picture, and I want to be clear there is no judgment here. What you have described is actually a **high-sodium intake, likely well over 3000-4000 mg per day**: canned beans, adobo, bouillon cubes, cured meats like ham and salami, and added table salt are all very concentrated sodium sources, and three cafe con leches plus soda is a substantial caffeine load. This matters enormously, because in your case sodium and caffeine are probably among the strongest drivers of your attack frequency. The reassuring flip side is that this is highly modifiable: we can keep the foods you love — rice, beans, sofrito, chicken — and simply swap to **no-salt-added or rinsed canned beans, salt-free adobo and sazon, low-sodium broth instead of bouillon, fresh chicken instead of ham or salami, and no salt at the table**. Reducing to **one caffeinated drink daily** and limiting alcohol gives us a strong nonpharmacologic foundation before we lean hard on medication.
That makes sense, and I feel a bit silly for not connecting it. I can do those swaps. So with the diet plus the medicines, what is my actual plan?

Please do not feel silly — most people genuinely do not realize how much sodium hides in everyday seasoning, and uncovering it is exactly why we did the recall. Here is your plan. One: **low-sodium diet under 2000 mg/day**, with the specific swaps we discussed, and reduce to one caffeinated beverage daily. Two: start **hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg with triamterene 37.5 mg once each morning**; I will check a basic metabolic panel in two weeks since thiazides can lower potassium and sodium — your baseline labs today are normal with **potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.1), sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145), and creatinine 0.8 mg/dL (0.6-1.1)**. Three: add **betahistine 16 mg three times daily**. Four: keep **meclizine 25 mg as a rescue** for attacks. Five: MRI with contrast, and vestibular testing. A critical safety point on the medications follows.
What is the safety concern? I want to take everything correctly.

Two interaction warnings. First, and most important for your future care: if we ever escalate to **intratympanic gentamicin** for refractory vertigo, gentamicin is ototoxic, and **loop diuretics such as furosemide dramatically potentiate that ototoxicity through shared cochlear toxicity, raising the risk of permanent deafness** — so we deliberately use a thiazide rather than furosemide, and you must tell any future clinician about this combination. Second, **betahistine is metabolized by monoamine oxidase, so MAO inhibitors can raise betahistine levels and prolong its effects** — let me confirm you are not taking any antidepressant of that class, including phenelzine or selegiline, or the supplement-type MAO inhibitors. Are you on any antidepressants, herbal products, or over-the-counter supplements?
No antidepressants and no MAO inhibitors. I take a daily multivitamin and sometimes ibuprofen for headaches, that is all. What if the diet and pills are not enough?

Good, no interaction concern there. If lifestyle, diuretic, and betahistine do not control your vertigo over two to three months, we escalate stepwise while protecting hearing. The next tier is **intratympanic dexamethasone** — a steroid injected through the eardrum that is hearing-preserving and reduces attacks in many patients. For truly refractory vertigo, **intratympanic gentamicin chemically ablates vestibular function and controls vertigo in roughly 80-90% of refractory cases**, but it carries a real risk of worsening hearing, so it is reserved for ears with already poor hearing or intractable attacks. Beyond that lie procedures: a **positive-pressure device (Meniett)**, **vestibular rehabilitation therapy**, **endolymphatic sac decompression**, hearing-sparing **vestibular nerve section**, and as a last resort the destructive **labyrinthectomy**, which sacrifices hearing in that ear. We would also fit a **hearing aid** as your low-frequency loss warrants. Since you mentioned ibuprofen, use it sparingly — NSAIDs can stress the kidneys alongside a diuretic. We will recheck labs and audiogram, and I will see you in four weeks with your MRI results.
Thank you, doctor. This is the first time I actually understand what is happening and feel like there is a path forward.

You are very welcome, Mariana. To summarize our shared plan: confirmed **definite right-sided Meniere's disease** pending MRI; a **low-sodium, low-caffeine diet** as your most powerful tool; daily **hydrochlorothiazide-triamterene** and **betahistine 16 mg three times daily**; **meclizine** for rescue; lab and audiogram monitoring; and a clear escalation ladder if needed. Keep a simple diary of attacks alongside your diet so we can see the sodium-attack relationship in your own data, do not drive during or right after an attack, and call urgently if you develop new severe headache, double vision, facial weakness, or sudden complete hearing loss. We will get this under control together.

turns.text: Hi doctor, I'm Daniel. I've been dealing with this gut stuff for about eight months now and it's getting hard to do my job. I drive long-haul, so I'm stuck in the cab for hours, and I get these cramps low in my belly that double me over. Some days I'm running to the bathroom three or four times with loose stools, other days I'm backed up for two or three days and it's like passing rocks. There's a ton of bloating too.

Thank you for laying that out so clearly, Daniel. That pattern of crampy lower abdominal pain with bowel habits swinging between loose and hard is exactly what I want to characterize precisely today. Let me anchor this with a few targeted questions. First, the pain itself: how often does it occur in a typical week, and what happens to it when you have a bowel movement? Does it get better, worse, or stay the same after you go?

The pain comes most days, honestly at least three or four days a week, sometimes daily. And yeah, when I finally have a bowel movement the cramp usually eases up for a while. It's like the pain and my bathroom habits are tied together. When the diarrhea is bad the stools are kind of mushy and shapeless, and when I'm constipated they come out as hard separate little lumps that are tough to pass.

That relationship between the pain and defecation is the cornerstone of what we look for. The **Rome IV criteria** for IBS require recurrent abdominal pain **at least 1 day per week, on average, over the last 3 months**, associated with two or more of the following: pain related to defecation, a change in stool frequency, or a change in stool form. You are describing pain most days that eases with defecation, with stools swinging between **Bristol type 6-7** (mushy, watery) and **Bristol type 1-2** (hard lumps). That comfortably satisfies the criteria. Before I commit to that, I need to rule out warning signs. Have you noticed any blood in your stool, black tarry stools, or any unintended weight loss?
No blood that I've seen, and no black stools. Weight has been pretty steady, maybe I've actually gained a few pounds from all the fast food on the road. No throwing up blood or anything like that.

Good, those are reassuring. Let me complete what we call the **alarm-feature screen**, because these are the features that would push me toward more aggressive workup like colonoscopy. Do you ever wake up from sleep at night because of the pain or to have a bowel movement? Any fevers? And on the family side, is there any history of inflammatory bowel disease such as Crohn's or ulcerative colitis, colon cancer, or celiac disease in your blood relatives?

I don't wake up at night for it, no. It's really a daytime thing, mostly when I'm driving and stressed. No fevers. As far as family, my mom has type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure, but nobody that I know of has the bowel diseases you mentioned or colon cancer. My grandfather did have stomach problems but I'm not sure what.

That is a clean alarm screen for a 34-year-old: no rectal bleeding, no nocturnal symptoms, no weight loss, no fevers, no clear family history of IBD, colorectal cancer, or celiac disease, and your onset is well before age 50. That profile makes a structural disease much less likely and supports a **positive diagnosis** rather than an open-ended hunt. Let me record your vitals and examine you. Your **BP is 128/80 mmHg, HR 76 bpm, temperature 36.8 C, SpO2 98%**, and your **BMI is 27.4**. On exam your abdomen is soft with mild tenderness in the left lower quadrant along the sigmoid, no guarding, no rebound, no palpable masses, normal bowel sounds, and your rectal exam shows no blood and normal tone. This is entirely consistent with IBS.
Okay, so if you're pretty sure it's IBS, do I still need a colonoscopy and a bunch of tests? My buddy got the full camera workup and it was miserable. I'd rather avoid it if I can.

I agree we should be judicious. Modern guidance, including the clinical review of Rome IV-based practice, favors a positive diagnosis with **limited, targeted testing** rather than exhaustive exclusion in someone young with no alarm features. For you I want a small panel: a **CBC** to check for anemia, a **CRP**, a **fecal calprotectin** to screen for inflammatory bowel disease, and **celiac serology (tissue transglutaminase IgA with a total IgA)**. Because your symptoms include diarrhea, calprotectin is particularly useful, as a normal value makes IBD very unlikely and spares you a colonoscopy. A colonoscopy would only be warranted if any alarm feature emerged or your calprotectin were elevated.
That sounds a lot more reasonable. Let's do those. While we wait, what's actually going on inside me? Is this all in my head? My last doctor kind of made it sound like I was just anxious.

It is absolutely not 'in your head,' and I want to be clear about that. IBS is a disorder of **gut-brain interaction**. The plumbing is structurally normal, but the signaling is dysregulated. Three mechanisms matter for you: **visceral hypersensitivity**, where normal amounts of gas and stretch are perceived as painful; altered gut motility, which drives the swing between diarrhea and constipation; and the **brain-gut axis**, where stress and the nervous system genuinely amplify gut signals. That is why your symptoms flare when you are stressed behind the wheel. There is also a role for the gut microbiome and intestinal permeability. The anxiety is not the cause of fake symptoms; it is one real input into a real biological loop. Your nervous system and your digestive system are wired together.
That actually makes sense and is a relief to hear. So how do we fix it? I can't be running to truck stop bathrooms all day, but I also can't be doubled over constipated.

We treat it in steps, and we tailor it to your subtype. Right now your bowel habits alternate, so you are **IBS-Mixed (IBS-M)** with prominent diarrhea episodes. Foundation first: dietary modification. The best-evidenced diet is a **low-FODMAP diet**, ideally with a dietitian, which reduces fermentable carbohydrates that drive your bloating and pain. I also want you to add **soluble fiber**, specifically psyllium, starting low at around 5 g daily and titrating up, because soluble fiber helps both the loose and the hard stool patterns, whereas insoluble bran can worsen bloating. For the cramps, an antispasmodic helps: **dicyclomine (Bentylol) 10 to 20 mg by mouth up to four times daily, taken before meals**. Take it as needed for crampy episodes rather than around the clock to limit dry mouth and blurred vision.
And for the diarrhea days specifically? When I have a run I have to drive, I can't be stopping every 30 minutes.

For acute diarrheal days, **loperamide (Imodium) 2 mg, two tablets at first loose stool then 2 mg after each subsequent loose stool, not exceeding 8 mg per day** without supervision, works well to control urgency and frequency. It does not treat the pain, so it pairs with the antispasmodic. One important safety point: never combine loperamide with **quinidine** or take large doses to get a high. Quinidine inhibits the P-glycoprotein pump and CYP2D6 that normally keep loperamide out of your brain and heart, and the combination can cause dangerous **respiratory depression and cardiac arrhythmias**. If your symptoms persist despite this, the targeted prescription option for IBS-D is **rifaximin (Xifaxan) 550 mg three times daily for 14 days**, a non-absorbed gut antibiotic. A meta-analysis of five trials showed adequate relief in 41% versus 32% on placebo, a number needed to treat of about 11.
What about when I swing the other way and get really constipated? Those are the days the pain is worst.

For the constipation-predominant flares, beyond fiber and hydration we have prescription secretagogues. **Linaclotide (Linzess) 290 mcg once daily, taken on an empty stomach at least 30 minutes before the first meal** increases intestinal fluid and speeds transit, and it also reduces the abdominal pain of IBS. An alternative is **lubiprostone (Amitiza) 8 mcg twice daily with food and water**. We would not run these at the same time as loperamide, since they pull in opposite directions; we deploy them based on which way you are swinging. Because you alternate, the practical approach is the daily foundation of low-FODMAP, psyllium, and dicyclomine, with loperamide kept on hand for diarrhea days and a secretagogue reserved if constipation becomes your dominant pattern.
One more thing. Since the stress angle is real, is there anything for that side of it? I don't love the idea of antidepressants though, I'm not depressed.

Fair, and the goal is not to treat depression. At **low doses, well below antidepressant dosing, a tricyclic such as amitriptyline 10 to 25 mg at bedtime** acts as a **neuromodulator**: it dampens visceral hypersensitivity and slows transit, which helps the IBS-D component and the pain. If constipation dominated, I would choose a low-dose SSRI instead. Equally evidence-based and drug-free are **gut-directed psychological therapies**, particularly cognitive behavioral therapy and gut-directed hypnotherapy, which directly retrain the brain-gut axis and have durable benefit. For a driver with stress-triggered flares, those are an excellent fit. We can start with diet, fiber, and as-needed agents, and layer in a neuromodulator or CBT if needed.
Sounds like a real plan. I'll start the low-FODMAP and the fiber. I've been pretty clean otherwise, I don't really drink and I'm not taking anything else, so no worries there.

I appreciate that, and I want to gently revisit it, because it matters for safety. Your intake form noted that you sometimes use **CBD gummies and an over-the-counter sleep aid**, and earlier you mentioned grabbing energy drinks to stay awake on long hauls. Those are not nothing for IBS. High caffeine intake from energy drinks is a potent gut stimulant that can drive both the urgency and the cramping, and some CBD and sleep products contain sorbitol or other sugar alcohols that are high-FODMAP and worsen bloating and diarrhea. There is no judgment here, but I need the full picture to give you safe advice. Can we go through what you are actually taking?

Okay, you got me, I should have mentioned it. Yeah, I do two or three big energy drinks a day on long routes, and the CBD gummies maybe a few nights a week to wind down. I didn't think they counted. So those could actually be making this worse?

Thank you for being straight with me, that genuinely changes the plan for the better. Two to three energy drinks daily is a large caffeine and sometimes sorbitol load that is very likely amplifying your diarrhea and cramps, so let us taper that down deliberately rather than cold turkey to avoid rebound headaches. Check the CBD gummy label for sorbitol, mannitol, or xylitol; if present, switch to a low-FODMAP alternative. Here is your written plan: start the **low-FODMAP diet** with a dietitian referral, **psyllium 5 g daily** titrating up, **dicyclomine 10-20 mg before meals as needed** for cramps, **loperamide 2 mg as directed for diarrheal days, never combined with quinidine**, and reserve **rifaximin 550 mg three times daily for 14 days** or **linaclotide 290 mcg daily** if symptoms persist by subtype. We will review the **calprotectin, CBC, CRP, and celiac serology** when they return, and if all are normal, as I expect, this confirms IBS-M and we avoid colonoscopy. Reduce the energy drinks, audit the gummies, and consider gut-directed CBT. Follow up in 4 weeks.

Quick question before I forget. My cousin takes something for a transplant, cyclosporine I think, and he also gets gut problems. If I ever needed that rifaximin, does any of my stuff interact with anything like that?

Good question, and it shows you are thinking about safety. **Rifaximin** is normally almost entirely non-absorbed, which is why it is so well tolerated. The one notable interaction is with **cyclosporine**, the transplant drug your cousin takes. Cyclosporine inhibits the **P-glycoprotein** transporter, which can raise rifaximin blood levels; this only becomes clinically meaningful if rifaximin loses its usual intestinal non-absorption. You are not on cyclosporine, so this does not apply to you, but it is exactly why I always take a full medication and supplement history, including the energy drinks and gummies we just discussed. Always tell any prescriber about every product you take, even the over-the-counter ones.
Got it, I'll keep a list from now on. And just to be sure, the loperamide for my diarrhea days, is the regular over-the-counter dose safe to keep in the truck?

Yes, kept within the standard dosing it is safe and effective: **2 mg at the first loose stool, then 2 mg after each subsequent loose stool, not exceeding 8 mg per day** for self-treatment. The danger is only with very high doses taken to chase a euphoric effect, or combining it with **quinidine** or similar P-glycoprotein and CYP2D6 inhibitors, which let it reach the brain and heart and risk **respiratory depression and life-threatening arrhythmias**. At normal doses, with no quinidine, keep it in the cab for diarrheal days alongside your dicyclomine for cramps. Stay hydrated, and do not stack it on days you are constipated.
Thank you, this is the first time I've actually understood what's wrong and felt like I have a way forward. I'll cut the energy drinks down and start the diet this week.

That is exactly the right mindset, Daniel. To summarize: you meet Rome IV criteria for **IBS, mixed subtype**, with a reassuring alarm-feature screen and a normal exam. We are confirming with limited targeted labs rather than an unnecessary colonoscopy. Your foundation is low-FODMAP diet, soluble fiber, and an antispasmodic, with subtype-specific agents on hand. Cutting the energy drinks and auditing the gummies will likely give you meaningful relief on its own. Call sooner if you develop any rectal bleeding, unintended weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, or fever, since those would change our approach. Otherwise I will see you in 4 weeks to review your labs and adjust.

turns.text: Hello doctor,I have PBC stage 4, Gave, COPD, Hashimoto\s, etc. I have been around someone who was just diagnosed with mono. I have used her water bottle. Should I be worried and, if so, what symptom could I develop? Do I have to stay away from this person now? I am currently under Urso 300 mg six per day.

Hello, Welcome to the ChatDoctor. I can understand your concern. Do not worry, and I will clear your doubt. Infectious mononucleosis usually caused by EBV (Epstein-Barr), and it can spread through saliva mainly. So sharing of the objects like water bottle or glass object can spread infection. So you are at risk of spending it. But do not be panic. The symptoms are fever and sore throat, mainly with enlarged cervical nodes. Splenomegaly also can occur. If fever, malaise, and sore throat occur than investigate by CBC (complete blood count) and serological test for EBV, which includes ESP (extrasensory perception), Ig M (immunoglobulin M), and Elisa (Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay). Infectious mononucleosis usually resolves by its own with time. Anyway if you suffer from fever and sore throat that will discuss further and you can consult a nearby physician for examination at that time. It is advisable not to share an object with an infected person. I hope this will help you. Get back with more query if you still have doubt.
